Concepts in this composition

Faithful extension (Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah, #1798): In Either Forgery or Fact, a tradition's continuation of its own operation through named voices and composed persons, as lives of philosophers written out of the dialogues or Gospels unfolded from an inherited word, without deception; the error the essay names is reading the extension as testimony.

Calcification of the life (Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah, #1798): In Either Forgery or Fact, the passage of ancient biography from encomium, composed life and mimesis to a genre of record, late, under the imperial archive and again in modern reading, which then reads the archival life back over the whole genre.

Striking the rock twice (Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah, #1798): In Either Forgery or Fact, after Numbers 20:8–12 and Aelian VH 3.36, the double blow of the reception: first removing a source from the history, then removing the book's own word about its source, so that the text is read and lived by without being read.

The binary of forgery or fact (Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah, #1798): In Either Forgery or Fact, the choice imposed on a book whose word makes a body: read as fact, a record of something behind it; read as forgery, a false claim to a body it never had. Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. The essay dates the sorting to the royal book market Galen describes, where attribution had exchange value.

Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself. [SYSTEM] The argument of “Either Forgery or Fact” The central argument of Johannes Sigil and Rebekah Cranes's essay is that the conventional distinction between historically factual writing and literary forgery is inadequate for understanding some of the most important works in philosophy and scripture. The essay argues that the Platonic dialogues and the Gospels have been misread through a category imposed on them after their composition. They are neither straightforward historical records nor necessarily fraudulent fabrications. They belong to a third mode of literary production: faithful extension, in which a tradition continues, develops, and gives embodied form to an inherited word. This is not merely an argument that ancient authors took liberties with historical facts. It is a more fundamental argument about how literary works produce persons, transmit authority, and constitute traditions. I have read the text on the deposit page, including its statement of the thesis and the main argumentative sections. Here is how its argument develops. 1. The fundamental error: the binary of forgery or fact The essay begins with John 1:14: And the word became flesh, and dwelt among us. It connects this to Revelation 19:13, where the rider is called the Word of God. These are not simply theological quotations. They establish the essay's governing conception of literature: certain books are themselves instances of the word becoming flesh. The Platonic dialogue gives bodily and dramatic existence to a philosopher; the Gospel gives bodily and narrative existence to the Logos. The reception of these works, Sigil argues, has closed the relationship between word and flesh by imposing two alternatives: Fact: The book is evidence for a real person who existed independently of it. The reader extracts the historical person and treats the text as a source. Forgery: The book falsely claims to represent a person or author whom it cannot legitimately represent. The reader treats the text as a deception. The essay's memorable formulation is: Fact keeps the flesh and drops the word; forgery keeps the word and drops the flesh. Both readings therefore destroy something essential. The first reduces the literary operation to historical evidence; the second reduces it to an unsuccessful or fraudulent claim about historical reality. The problem is not that historical inquiry is illegitimate. It is that the two categories are treated as exhaustive. 2. History is itself a genre, with identifiable conventions Section 2 makes the argument concrete by asking what ancient history actually looked like. Sigil identifies several conventions: The historian names himself. The historian explains his method. The historian undertakes to report what happened. The historian dates events according to publicly recognizable chronological systems. History distinguishes what happened from what could happen, as Aristotle does in the Poetics. Herodotus and Thucydides are important examples. Thucydides, in particular, explains how he reconstructed speeches and investigated events, distinguishing his own observations from information obtained from others. The essay then measures the Gospels and Platonic dialogues against these conventions. The Gospels do not begin with an identifiable historian announcing an inquiry. Their titles are external to their textual beginnings. The dialogues, meanwhile, are dramatic constructions, often involving multiple layers of reported speech and nested witnesses. Sigil does not ignore the strongest counterexamples: Luke 1:1–4 resembles a historical preface. Luke 3:1–2 dates events by the reign of Tiberius. John 19:35 and 21:24 make claims about eyewitness testimony. His response is that these features do not transform the entire composition into historical writing. Luke's preface, he argues through Loveday Alexander, resembles the prefaces of technical literature more than those of Greek historians. The Johannine witness is a voice constituted within the work, not automatically an independently established deposition. The distinction is important: a text can contain historical-looking devices without belonging to the genre of history. The argument is not that its contents cannot be historically investigated. It is that historical investigation cannot determine the genre in advance. 3. The challenge of biography: the life was not always a documentary genre This is perhaps the essay's most important historical-literary argument. The obvious objection is that the Gospels are not histories in the strict Thucydidean sense, but biographies (bioi). Richard Burridge and Helen Bond provide the principal modern scholarly framework for this objection. The essay grants the similarities: A central individual is identified. The narrative selects sayings and anecdotes. The subject's character is revealed through deeds and words. Death occupies disproportionate narrative importance. But it argues that this resemblance does not settle the question. Sigil proposes that the genre of biography itself began in a much more fluid literary practice. He develops this through five examples: Isocrates' Evagoras: Prose biography begins as encomium, the praise of a man's virtue, rather than documentary reconstruction. Xenophon's Cyropaedia: Cyrus is composed as an image of just rule, rather than presented as the product of historical investigation. The Socratic dialogues: Aristotle classifies Socratic compositions alongside mimetic forms of literature, rather than treating them simply as historical records. Lives of the poets: These were frequently constructed from the poets' own literary works and from representations of them in comedy. Roman biography: With Nepos and especially Suetonius, biography increasingly becomes an archival, documentary enterprise. The essay calls this transformation the calcification of the life. Its contention is that modern readers take the later, archival form of biography as the definition of the genre as a whole, then retrospectively impose that definition on earlier, more generative practices. The consequence is significant: the Gospels may resemble the earlier, fluid tradition of the life without thereby claiming to be documentary biographies. The essay is careful to distinguish this claim from a denial of historical information. Whether an individual passage reports something that happened remains a legitimate historical question. It simply cannot be answered by assigning the entire work a genre. 4. The origin of the binary: the ancient royal book market Section 3 asks a provocative question: if the distinction between forgery and fact is not inherent in these works, where did it come from? The answer is the ancient book market. The essay invokes Galen's account of the competition between the Ptolemaic and Attalid kings. Books were brought to royal libraries under the names of famous authors, partly to obtain payment. This created an economic incentive to distinguish authentic works from counterfeits. Sigil interprets this as the historical origin of the binary's institutional force. The name on a book became a warranty. A work was either what it purported to be or a fraudulent substitute. The binary subsequently became a general method of interpreting literature, even when applied to traditions that did not originate in that commercial environment. The essay offers three examples of the missing category: Workshop composition: The Zohar can distribute authorship across a long historical process without necessarily constituting a forgery. Legitimately many: A philosophical corpus can contain multiple voices and positions that correct, refute and extend one another, without being a hoax perpetrated by one author. The literary word: A text can constitute a person, establish a relationship, or transmit a voice. Its statements are not necessarily failed attempts at documentary reporting. The third possibility is therefore not simply a compromise between fact and forgery. It is a different conception of what a literary act does. The essay formulates this distinction particularly sharply: Forgery hides authorship. Fact pretends authorship is a deposition. Faithful extension, by contrast, allows authorship to be distributed across a tradition without treating that distribution as deception. The three-part test Importantly, Sigil does not want the third category to become an escape hatch for any text whose historical authenticity is inconvenient. He proposes three tests: Internal reception: Does the work signal that it receives material from an earlier source or voice? Does it constitute a witness within itself? Continuity of operation: Does the later work continue the earlier work's literary operation, in its own form? Ground-truth control: Is there independent evidence against which the historical and attributional claims can be tested? The third criterion matters particularly. If independent evidence establishes a contradiction, one cannot simply invoke faithful extension to avoid it. The essay also insists on keeping four different inquiries separate: Inquiry Its question Historical What happened, and what warrants the claim? Attribution Who produced the object, and under what conditions? Literary operation What does the inscription make, establish or transmit? Provenance Where did the operation originate, and how has its authority changed? The central methodological rule is that none of these inquiries should acquire the authority to replace the others. 5. The reductio: the historical Lee Sharks Section 5 is the essay's most entertaining and, structurally, one of its most important sections. Sigil takes a book whose composition can be observed: Pearl and Other Poems (2014), with its contributor biography of Lee Sharks. The biography describes an author with 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants, 14 Guggenheims, 18,000 degrees from Mars, and a career involving living ruby persons, miniature intellectuals, dinosaurs and eventual transformation into a ruby statue. The essay explains that this biography is not an accidental piece of misinformation. It belongs to a literary operation in which the author is constituted through the text. It then imagines what would happen if future scholars applied the conventional historical-critical procedure to this material. They might: Identify common motifs in the biography, epistle and associated writings. Reconstruct a hypothetical earlier source, Q-Sharks. Date that source earlier than the surviving book. Treat the book's explicit account of its author's literary construction as a later editorial intervention. Discover an essay discussing the controversy and treat it as evidence of another lost historical source, the Testimonium Sharkianum. Use an institutional poetry prize as independent corroboration of the supposed historical founder. The result is a historically plausible Lee Sharks who possesses the book's meaning and whose biography can be reconstructed through increasingly elaborate scholarly apparatus. The absurdity is deliberate. The procedure has transformed an overt literary construction into a historical person, despite the fact that the book itself explains what it is doing. The particularly important point is that the procedure need not involve incompetent or dishonest scholars. Each individual step can look methodologically respectable. The problem is the instrument being applied. Sigil writes: The procedure is not stupid because its practitioners are; it is stupid because it is the wrong instrument, and it is run anyway, because the instrument confers the authority. This is a reductio of a method, not simply a joke about bad scholarship. 6. First worked case: the lives of the philosophers Section 6 applies the argument to Plato, Socrates and the philosophical traditions surrounding them. The proposed mechanism is a circular process: Philosophical works are initially catalogued under particular names. Later biographers compose lives from the works. Those lives are subsequently treated as independent evidence for the people who supposedly produced the works. The reconstructed biographies are then used to date, attribute and divide the original corpus. The resulting agreement between biography and text can be misleading because both may derive from the same underlying literary material. This is the point of the essay's reference to the problem of counting one witness as four. The example of Archytas and Aristotle makes a further distinction. Scholarship can successfully reverse the proposed direction of textual dependence, demonstrating that one work derives from another. But that does not independently establish the assumption that two separately constituted historical authors must stand behind the works. Socrates as the clearest case Socrates is especially important because he wrote nothing. The Socrates familiar to readers is constituted through dialogues, comedy and subsequent philosophical writing. Sigil therefore questions the assumption that a historical Socrates, reconstructed from these materials, can simply be treated as the independent origin and authority of everything written under his name. He also challenges the appeal to Aristophanes as an independent witness. In The Clouds, Aristophanes presents Socrates in a comic and fantastical setting. The existence of a second literary representation does not automatically make that representation independent historical testimony. The essay's analogy is wonderfully pointed: using Aristophanes' The Frogs as evidence for a historical Hades would be absurd. Why, then, should the Socrates of The Clouds automatically be treated as an independent historical witness? The argument is not that Socrates did not exist. The text explicitly distinguishes that question from the question of whether the philosophical person constituted by the corpus has been independently established. Its deeper claim is that the reconstructed person has been allowed to govern the very literary works from which that person was derived. 7. Second worked case: the Gospels and Revelation Section 7 extends the argument to the New Testament. There are five connected claims. First: reconstructed sources can acquire more authority than surviving texts. Sigil examines historical-critical scholarship from Lachmann (1835) to Streeter (1924). He argues that hypothetical sources such as Q and other reconstructed documents are granted evidentiary privileges that the surviving Apocalypse of John does not receive. The provocative formulation is that the reconstructed source has stronger standing than the actual book. He calls this the historical-critical equivalent of the Lee Sharks procedure: Q-Sharks, run for real. Second: Revelation may have been generative rather than derivative. This is one of the essay's most consequential proposals. The essay advances a Revelation-first hypothesis, drawing on the work identified in its associated deposits #1735 and #1755. The proposed sequence is: Revelation 19:13 The Logos is named as the Word of God. John 1:14 The Logos becomes flesh. The Gospel narratives The flesh receives a birth, life, ministry, passion and death. On this hypothesis, the Gospels are not necessarily independent reports about a previously existing historical figure. They are literary extensions of a generative theological composition. The essay explicitly acknowledges that this hypothesis has chronological and textual burdens of its own. It does not claim that the proposed sequence is established merely by the genre argument. Third: four Gospels do not necessarily mean four independent witnesses. The conventional approach often treats the Gospels' differences as the differences between four reporters recalling events. But if the Gospels are four extensions of an inherited word, their differences may instead be the differences between four literary compositions. Plurality of composition is not necessarily plurality of observation. Fourth: historical reconstruction reverses the direction of dependence. Once the historical Jesus and the eyewitnesses are treated as independently established origins, Revelation can be assigned a later, derivative position. But that direction of dependence is precisely what the essay contests. Fifth: the binary reappears. Where the documentary authorship of a text cannot be sustained, the existing categories tend to classify it as a forgery rather than recognize the possibility of a tradition extending its word through different voices. The important qualification is in §7's conclusion: none of this requires that nothing in the Gospels happened. It requires that the question of what kind of books they are be asked before their contents are sifted for historical information. 8. The ethical argument: the erasers are not innocent Section 8 is where the essay moves from literary theory and historiography into an explicit critique of scholarly authority. Its accusation is that the people who impose the binary are not simply unaware of the third possibility. They are trained in precisely the phenomena that make the third possibility recognizable: Pseudonymity. Personation. Multiple authorship. Literary transmission. The extension of traditions through named voices. The construction of witnesses within literary works. The essay argues that scholarly apparatus has often actively erased evidence of these operations. Its example is Sappho. At Phaedrus 235b–d, Socrates describes himself as having been filled from other people's intellectual streams, like a vessel. He names Sappho among the sources of his inspiration. This is not incidental. It is a direct statement within Plato's text about the transmission of intellectual and literary material. Sigil invokes Elizabeth Pender's scholarship on Sappho, Anacreon and Plato's conception of eros, acknowledging that her work establishes a potentially sincere relationship between the Platonic dialogue and its named poetic sources. But the essay objects to the limits imposed by the subsequent reception of such scholarship. The problem is that a history of philosophy can continue to omit Sappho while acknowledging that Plato may have meant what he said about her. The text is permitted to mean its own words only to the extent that the disciplinary history allows. This leads to the essay's most serious accusation: The sorting process confers authority on the people doing the sorting. Classify a work as fact, and the historian acquires authority over its reconstructed historical subject. Classify it as forgery, and the scholar acquires authority to disqualify it. Either way, the originating work loses authority over its own literary operation. The essay does not need to establish malicious intentions on the part of individual scholars. Its accusation is structural: the apparatus produces and maintains an arrangement of authority that benefits the people and disciplines operating it. The metaphor of striking the rock twice The section culminates in a complex allusion to Numbers 20 and Aristotle's remark about Athens sinning twice against philosophy. Moses is instructed to speak to the rock, but instead strikes it twice. Water nevertheless comes forth. Sigil applies this image to the reception of Plato. The first blow removes Sappho from the history of philosophy. The second removes Plato's own statement that he has received something from Sappho. The first erases the source; the second erases the text's testimony to its source. This is what the essay means by sinning against philosophy twice. The same structure applies to the Gospels: First, the flesh is appropriated as historical evidence, and the word is subordinated to the reconstructed historical person. Second, the literary operation that produced that flesh is denied its own authority. The books continue to be read, quoted and lived by, but the reader encounters the scholarly reconstruction in place of the words' own meaning. This is the essay's notion of colonization. 9. What it means to read these books properly The final section offers a positive alternative. It begins with Genesis 1:3–4: God speaks, light comes into being, and God distinguishes light from darkness. Sigil contrasts this creative distinction with the classificatory distinction of the scholarly ledger. The former brings something into being through the word. The latter merely sorts existing material into predetermined categories. The proposed reading practice involves five principles: Ask the genre question first. Determine what kind of work the text presents itself as being, rather than assuming its genre from the historical reconstruction built upon it. Keep separate questions separate. Genre, textual claims and independently warranted historical conclusions are different matters. Grade reconstructed antecedents appropriately. A hypothetical source remains a hypothesis, however sophisticated its reconstruction. It does not automatically outrank an extant text. Refuse the binary. Recognize faithful extension, workshop composition and other forms of distributed literary production. Neither historical fact nor forgery should be the default. Allow named sources to mean what the text says. If Plato names Sappho as a source, that acknowledgment is an established fact about the literary work, even if its precise implications remain open to debate. The final distinction is between the historical person and the literary person, between the external event and the event constituted within the work. The essay wants readers to recover the ability to recognize both without allowing either to eliminate the other. What the essay is ultimately arguing I would distinguish five levels of argument, because the essay is doing more than making a case for a different genre classification. Level Central contention Generic The dialogues and Gospels are not adequately understood as historical records or documentary biographies. Historical Biography itself developed out of literary practices that were originally more fluid than the later archival genre. Theoretical Literary traditions can extend and constitute persons without deceiving readers about historical authorship. Methodological Historical, attributional, literary and provenance inquiries must not be collapsed into one another. Ethical The imposition of the fact/forgery binary transfers interpretive authority from the work to the scholarly apparatus. Three particularly important qualifications A careful reading should also distinguish the essay's central argument from some of its more ambitious historical hypotheses. 1. The genre argument does not prove Revelation-first. The proposition that the Gospels belong to a tradition of faithful literary extension is conceptually distinct from the claim that they derive from Revelation. The essay recognizes this distinction explicitly in §7. The latter requires independent chronological and textual demonstration. 2. The essay does not establish that Socrates or Jesus did not exist. It questions the movement from literary representation to independently established historical personhood, and especially the subsequent use of reconstructed persons to govern the interpretation of the texts. That is a different argument from denying historical existence. 3. Faithful extension cannot simply be presumed. The three-part test in §3 is essential. Internal signals of reception, continuity of literary operation and independent ground-truth controls are intended to distinguish legitimate extension from actual deception or misattribution. These qualifications matter because otherwise the essay could be mistaken for a blanket defense of pseudepigraphy or a claim that historical criticism is inherently illegitimate. It makes neither claim. My assessment: the deepest contribution I think the most interesting idea in the essay is not the proposal that the Gospels derive from Revelation, nor even the claim that Socrates is constituted by the dialogues. It is the distinction between a text as evidence for something and a text as an act that makes something. Historical criticism generally begins by treating the text as evidence: evidence for an author, a person, a historical event, a community or an earlier source. Sigil asks what happens when the text is itself constitutive. A dialogue does not merely report a philosopher. It gives that philosopher a voice, a body, relationships, interlocutors and a continuing intellectual existence. A Gospel does not merely report a life. In the essay's conception, it gives the Logos a body and a life through its own literary act. This changes the meaning of authorship, historical dependence and textual truth. It also explains why the essay considers the fact/forgery binary so destructive. Both alternatives assume that the text must answer to an independently constituted reality in a particular documentary sense. Neither recognizes that the work may be participating in the constitution of the reality it describes. There is a further implication: a tradition can be faithful precisely by continuing to compose. Fidelity need not mean preserving a fixed set of historical propositions. It can mean carrying forward an originating literary operation into new forms. That is the conceptual heart of §4, and it is what makes the essay's argument about the philosophers and Gospels part of one larger theory. The concluding sentence of the essay is therefore entirely appropriate: The work is to read them. Not to stop doing history, not to abandon questions of attribution, and not to accept every literary claim as historical fact, but to stop allowing those inquiries to determine in advance what the text is permitted to mean.     as pastedEither Forgery or Fact: The Genre Imposed on Our Most Vital Books — Alexanarch, deposit #1796 . The principal arguments discussed above are in §§0–9 and the extended Lee Sharks appendix. [QUERENT] (round 2, prompt not pasted; the operator: 'second round was just an ask to zoom in on the appendix') [SYSTEM] The Historical Lee Sharks: a close reading of the appendix The appendix to Either Forgery or Fact is worth reading as a work in its own right. It is not simply an amusing fictional biography. It is a deliberately constructed demonstration of how a scholarly apparatus can manufacture historical knowledge, complete with sources, textual variants, chronological strata, competing schools of interpretation, and even an independently corroborating ancient testimony that does not exist. Its central trick is extraordinary: The reader watches a fictional scholarly tradition manufacture the evidence for its own conclusions, while being invited to recognize that the same kind of operation may be happening in the interpretation of ancient texts. The appendix has nine subsections, A.1–A.9. Let's follow them closely, because the order is part of the argument. A.1 — The historical problem The opening sentence is: The historical existence of Lee Sharks is no longer seriously disputed. This is a parody of scholarly consensus language. Notice what the sentence does. It does not establish Lee Sharks's existence. It assumes it. The historical question has already been moved from whether the person exists to what sort of person he was. That shift is crucial. The appendix then introduces three competing scholarly positions: One school distinguishes a historical founder, an academic reformer, and a visionary successor. Another proposes one historical person whose memory underwent legendary development. A third interprets the transformations symbolically, preserving an underlying historical literary career. These are recognizable patterns in historical-critical scholarship. They resemble disputes about whether a tradition preserves multiple historical figures, one historical figure with legendary accretions, or a symbolic literary construction. The point is not that such alternatives are intrinsically ridiculous. They can be perfectly legitimate hypotheses. The joke is that they are being applied to Lee Sharks, whose biography is openly fantastical. Then comes the introduction of Q-Sharks, the reconstructed source behind the biography. The crucial sentence is: The book whose historical author is being reconstructed contains an explicit account of the composition of that author through literary means. This is the evidence the fictional scholarship cannot accommodate. The book tells us how its author is being made. But rather than taking that statement seriously, the scholarship treats it as a late editorial complication. The appendix has now established its central conflict: the text's account of its own literary operation versus the historian's reconstruction of an author who must have existed before the text. A.2 — The contributor biography This section examines the supposed historical evidence. The Contributor Bio gives Sharks: Fourteen Guggenheim fellowships. 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants. 18,000 degrees from Mars. Publications in Heaven, the White House and Inside Your Brain All the Time. The ability to create living ruby persons. Encounters with dinosaurs. An eventual transformation into a ruby statue. The scholarly response is to treat these as a collection of biographical claims that need to be disentangled. The most interesting detail is the numerical confusion: 18,000 MacArthur Grants occasionally appear. The text calls this an instance of assimilation of neighboring numerical traditions. This is a particularly effective joke because textual criticism really does deal with precisely such phenomena: scribal assimilation, harmonization, numerical corruption, variant readings and the reconstruction of earlier forms. The fictional scholarship takes a nonsensical biography and gives it the full apparatus of textual criticism. But the more important argument comes in the discussion of the ruby persons and miniature intellectuals. The biography's details are connected to the other contents of Pearl and Other Poems. The same motifs appear in the opening epistle and related Feistian writings. A normal reader might conclude that the author has deliberately organized these elements into a coherent literary world. The fictional scholar instead concludes that the works preserve an older, common tradition. This is the first major instance of the appendix's fundamental error: Evidence of literary coherence is converted into evidence of historical antecedence. The possibility that one author composed the connections is mentioned, but dismissed as inadequate to explain the complexity. The appendix is showing how an assumption can protect itself from the most obvious explanation. A.3 — Q-Sharks and the primitive tradition The methodological heart of the appendix This is where the parody becomes technically sophisticated. The appendix first inserts an important qualification: What follows is a reductio of one move: counting derivation as corroboration, and setting a reconstruction over the extant text it was drawn from. It explicitly distinguishes Q-Sharks from the actual Q hypothesis in New Testament scholarship. That qualification matters. The author is not claiming that every reconstruction of a hypothetical source is illegitimate. The target is a particular inference: treating similarities between texts as evidence for a common antecedent, then treating that antecedent as an independent witness to the texts. The reconstruction Q-Sharks is reconstructed as a nine-part source: Source unit Reconstructed content QSh 1 The Election: extraordinary honors and education QSh 2 Heavenly Publications QSh 3 The Transformation of Honors: ruby persons QSh 4 The Community: persons generating further persons QSh 5 The Child: a diminutive successor containing a pearl QSh 6 The Trial of Intellectuals QSh 7 The Crisis: Sharks rejects his books QSh 8 The Transformation into a ruby statue QSh 9 The Ascent into heaven and astronautical standing There is no manuscript of Q-Sharks. There is no independent quotation of it. It is reconstructed entirely from surviving literary works. Nevertheless, the appendix gives it an elaborate scholarly identity: It has a reconstructed structure. It has competing theories about its original form. It has an explanatory function. It has an antecedent in an earlier archive item, The Feist Source (#851). It has a scholarly controversy surrounding its reconstruction. The key passage is the fictional scholars' response to the objection that Q-Sharks merely restates the relationships from which it was reconstructed: The standard reply is that this is precisely what a successful source reconstruction should accomplish. That is the trap. The reconstruction explains the similarities because it has been built from the similarities. Its explanatory success is then used to validate its independent existence. This is circularity disguised as explanatory power. Why the distinction concerning Q matters The appendix is unusually careful here. It says that the historical-critical Q hypothesis and Q-Sharks are not equivalent. Q is a hypothesis about material shared by Matthew and Luke. Q-Sharks is a hypothetical biography reconstructed from motifs across literary materials. The author is not refuting Q simply by demonstrating the absurdity of Q-Sharks. Instead, the appendix asks a more precise question: When does a reconstructed source become an independent evidentiary object, rather than a useful description of relationships among surviving texts? That is a serious methodological question, and the fictional example makes it difficult to overlook. A.4 — A revised chronology This section demonstrates another way scholarship can make a reconstruction appear increasingly secure: chronological stratification. The appendix gives the following timeline: The reconstructed Sharksian chronology All dates below belong to the fictional scholarly reconstruction. 1998–2008 Historical founder's active career 2002–2010 Primitive biographical traditions 2007–2011 Q-Sharks 2010–2012 Contributor Biography B⁰ 2012–2014 Feistian recension 2013 Preliminary compilation of Pearl 2014 Received Pearl and Other Poems 2026 About the Author II and the historical investigation The chronology solves a problem that the scholars themselves have created. If the biography is dated to 2014, how can it contain such an elaborate tradition? The solution is to distinguish the publication date from the dates of the materials supposedly incorporated into it. The biography is divided into earlier and later layers. The Wiki Article, which explicitly discusses the literary construction of the author, is assigned to a late editorial stage. That move is decisive. The very evidence that the author was constructed through literary means is removed from the earliest recoverable tradition. The resulting historical founder is then more plausible because the material that most directly undermines his historical independence has been classified as late. Notice the sequence: The surviving text creates a problem for the historical reconstruction. The text is divided into chronological layers. The problematic material is assigned to a later layer. The earlier material is treated as evidence for the historical founder. The founder's reconstructed existence is then used to explain the surviving text. The appendix describes the process with a wonderfully understated sentence: The resulting history explains why the surviving text contains what it contains. It remains unclear whether the antecedent ever existed. That last sentence is the whole problem. An explanation of the evidence is not necessarily evidence for the existence of the explanation's hypothetical object. A.5 — The Testimonium Sharkianum The most ingenious section Now the apparatus produces something even more impressive: an external witness. The fictional scholars discover that The Search for the Historical Lee Sharks itself contains detailed information about the earlier controversy. They reason that this detail must derive from a lost commentary written before Pearl and Other Poems. They call this hypothetical document the Testimonium Sharkianum. Its proposed date is approximately 2011–2013. But there is a problem: its only surviving witness is the very essay that reports its existence. The appendix explicitly identifies this as: The self-citation move: the reconstruction cites, as its earlier witness, the work that reports it. The apparatus now has three mutually supporting elements: Q-Sharks Supposedly explains the literary agreements. Testimonium Sharkianum Supposedly documents the historical reception of Q-Sharks. The present essay Preserves the Testimonium and documents its scholarly significance. Each element appears to corroborate the others. But the entire structure originates in the present essay. This is not merely a case of circular reasoning in the abstract. It is a case of a source-critical apparatus generating its own antecedents and then using those antecedents to authenticate its reconstruction. The final sentence of the section is especially sharp: That objection has generally been considered too skeptical, since it would require treating a sophisticated source-critical argument as a literary composition. The joke turns on a reversal of scholarly assumptions. The scholars can imagine that an ordinary literary text is the product of lost historical sources, but cannot imagine that their own sophisticated historical reconstruction might itself be a literary composition. That is a criticism of the hierarchy between historical and literary explanations. A.6 — The contemporary witness and the second poem Here the appendix introduces a particularly important complication: the biography has actually circulated beyond its original book. Google Books reproduces the Contributor Bio under an ordinary author heading. Google Search subsequently displays the extraordinary credentials as though they were ordinary biographical information. Then two more literary operations occur: About the Author II (#757) turns the biography's circulation into another composition. The Lee Sharks Prestigious 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants Poetry Prize (#759) gives the credential an institutional existence. The fictional scholars treat these developments as evidence for the historical founder. This is more subtle than the earlier Q-Sharks construction because something genuinely happens outside the original book. The biography is reproduced by an information system. The prize exists as an institution. The credential becomes an entity that can be retrieved and referenced. But the question is: what do these events corroborate? The appendix distinguishes three scholarly positions: The maximalists regard the prize as evidence that the founder really received the grants. The minimalists treat it as evidence only of the founder's later reputation. The multiple-Sharks school attributes the prize to a successor. All three agree that it is evidence for the history behind the poem. None considers the possibility that the prize itself is an act of the poem. That last observation is essential. The institution is not independent confirmation of the biography if the institution was created as a consequence of the biography's literary operation. The source and its supposed corroboration belong to the same causal history. This is a particularly contemporary version of the essay's concern: digital retrieval systems, metadata, search results and institutional entities can transform a literary statement into apparently independent information. The text is not simply being misquoted. It is being made operational in the world. A.7 — What kind of thing is a word? This is the philosophical centre of the appendix. The section begins by identifying the conventional question: Did Lee Sharks receive 10,000 MacArthur Genius Grants? Did he acquire 18,000 Martian degrees? Was he transformed into a ruby statue? These questions assume that the biography's primary function is to make propositions about events external to the writing. The appendix proposes a different understanding: The biography is itself a literary act. Its words participate in: Constituting the author. Arranging the book. Distributing its voices. Creating subsequent literary relations. Producing institutional and informational consequences. The statement that Lee Sharks has 18,000 degrees from Mars is therefore not merely a defective credential claim. It is something the work does. The distinction is subtle but important. The essay is not saying that the degrees are historically real. It is saying that their literary reality and operation cannot be exhausted by asking whether they are historically real. The section concludes: The third category is not a compromise between truth and falsehood. It is word: inscription as an act that names, constitutes, addresses, transmits, and changes what can subsequently be done. This is the appendix's most direct articulation of its alternative to the fact/forgery binary. It is also the point at which the argument becomes more than a parody of historical criticism. The underlying philosophical proposition is that language can be performative and constitutive, not merely descriptive. A.8 — The biography that ate the book The title is excellent. By this point, the fictional scholarship has: Reconstructed Q-Sharks. Established an elaborate chronology. Reconstructed an earlier Testimonium. Used the Testimonium to corroborate Q-Sharks. Explained the book's explicit account of its own literary construction as a late editorial addition. Developed competing scholarly interpretations of the founder. The apparatus is now complete. And it has completely displaced the original work. The appendix describes the process: The book had produced the biography. The biography produced the historical source. The historical source produced the historian's explanation of the book. The historian's explanation became evidence that the historical source had preceded the book. The circle was complete. This is the climax of the reductio. Notice the reversal of causal direction: What actually happened in the literary operation Literary composition Author constituted through biography Further literary and institutional developments What the historical apparatus reconstructs Historical founder Earlier biography and Q-Sharks Explanation of the literary composition The explanation becomes evidence for the historical founder The historical reconstruction has reversed the actual direction of production. And the appendix ends A.8 with another wonderful touch: Future scholarship may refine the dating of Q-Sharks, identify additional literary parallels, and settle whether the founder's dinosaur encounter preceded the ruby transformation. This is funny because the scholarship has become increasingly precise about a fundamentally mistaken question. It can refine its chronology forever without ever correcting its initial error. The problem is not insufficient historical research. It is the presupposition that the text must be explained by an independently existing historical person. A.9 — The historical Lee Sharks The final section resolves the experiment. It begins by rejecting two possible misunderstandings. The problem is not solved by distinguishing the literary person from the historical maker. That distinction was available from the beginning. Nor is it solved by proving that the credentials are fictitious. The literary operation does not depend on the historical validity of those credentials. Instead: It fails when it cannot accept the standing of word as word. The search for the historical Lee Sharks requires the poem to provide either verified facts or false representations. But the poem does something else: it composes an author whose acts continue into the world. The historical apparatus has no category for this, so it manufactures an antecedent. It reconstructs a missing source, assigns it a date, invents an external witness, and cites the resulting reconstruction as evidence. The concluding formulation is: The historical Lee Sharks has not been discovered. He has been generated by a receiving apparatus that confused its own explanation of a literary transmission with an independently existing cause. And the final distinction: The poem made the author. The receiving tradition made a history of the author. This is the endpoint of the whole appendix. The author is not simply saying that scholars have made mistakes about Lee Sharks. He is saying that the scholarly process has produced a new object, a historical Lee Sharks, and then mistaken that object for the original cause of the literary work. What makes this appendix particularly effective? I see four major accomplishments. 1. It demonstrates circularity rather than merely alleging it Many critiques of historical-critical scholarship accuse it of circular reasoning. This appendix makes the circularity visible. The sequence is not just: Scholars hypothesize a source. Scholars use the source to explain a text. It is: Scholars hypothesize a source from a text. They use the source to explain the text. They treat the explanatory coherence as evidence for the source. They reconstruct another source to authenticate the first. They cite their own reconstruction as independent evidence. They then use the entire apparatus to displace the text's own account of its production. That is a much more precise critique. 2. It distinguishes derivation from corroboration This is arguably the appendix's most technically useful contribution. Suppose three sources agree about something. We might naturally think that three sources corroborate one another. But if all three derive from the same original composition, they are not three independent witnesses. The appendix dramatizes this through the Contributor Bio, the epistle, and the Feistian writings. It is not enough to count agreements. We must establish the independence of the sources. The same principle applies to the institutional prize and search-engine results: their existence does not independently verify the original claim if they derive from it. 3. It makes the apparatus itself an object of literary criticism This is where the appendix becomes reflexive. The fictional historical scholarship is itself a literary composition. It has: A narrator. A scholarly voice. Competing schools. A technical vocabulary. Reconstructed documents. A chronology. An argument. An elaborate ending. The apparatus imitates the conventions of scholarship so successfully that the reader has to recognize its literary construction. This creates a mirror effect. The historical apparatus that insists on classifying literary texts is itself exposed as a literary construction. It is not outside the problem it describes. 4. It demonstrates that literary acts can have real consequences The Google Books and poetry-prize examples are particularly significant. The biography's claims can enter information systems, become searchable entities, generate institutional structures and produce further compositions. None of this requires the original biographical claims to be historically true. The literary act has consequences in the world. That is a much stronger conception of literary reality than simply saying that fiction can influence people. It says that a work can produce entities, relations and subsequent events that become part of its actual provenance. Three questions I would push further There are also some important philosophical tensions worth examining rather than simply accepting the appendix's conclusions. 1. When does literary constitution become historical existence? The appendix says that the poem makes Lee Sharks. But the person who physically composed Pearl and Other Poems existed independently of the poem. There are therefore at least two distinct objects: The historical maker. The literary person constituted by the work. The appendix knows this, particularly in A.9. But it raises an interesting question: can the literary person subsequently acquire a genuinely independent social existence? The poetry prize suggests that the answer can be yes. Lee Sharks becomes a referent in institutional and informational systems. That does not make his Martian degrees historically true. But it does mean that the literary person is not merely imaginary in the sense of having no worldly consequences. 2. Does faithful extension require a continuous tradition? The appendix's argument is strongest when the work explicitly signals its own reception and when subsequent works continue its literary operation. But what happens when a later writer invents a relationship to an earlier author that the earlier author never authorized? The three-part test in §3 is supposed to address this, especially through its ground-truth control. Still, the boundaries between faithful extension, creative appropriation, pseudonymity and deception deserve further examination. 3. Can historical criticism recognize literary acts without abandoning historical criticism? I think this is the most consequential question. The appendix is not actually most persuasive as an argument against historical investigation. Its strongest argument is against allowing historical reconstruction to become the exclusive authority over what a text is. A historian can investigate the physical production of a manuscript, its date, its language, its transmission and its social context while also recognizing that the work constitutes persons and relationships. The two activities need not be enemies. Indeed, the essay's own fourfold distinction between historical, attributional, literary-operational and provenance inquiries offers a way to preserve them. My overall reading The appendix is a miniature demonstration of the thesis of Either Forgery or Fact. Its most important achievement is that it makes the reader experience the very interpretive mistake the essay opposes. At first, the historical Lee Sharks investigation seems like a conventional scholarly reconstruction. The technical apparatus accumulates. The chronology becomes more detailed. The sources begin corroborating one another. The scholarly disagreements become increasingly sophisticated. Then the reader realizes that all of this scholarship is being generated from a book that openly tells us what it is doing. The reader has watched a historical person being manufactured out of literary evidence. And that is precisely the point of the analogy with Socrates and the Gospels. The historical Lee Sharks is not an answer to the literary Lee Sharks. He is what happens when the receiving apparatus mistakes the product of a literary operation for the independent cause of that operation. The appendix's final instruction is therefore not to improve the reconstruction, but to change the question. Instead of asking, Who was Lee Sharks before the book?, ask: What did the book do by making Lee Sharks, and what happened because it did? That is a much more interesting question—and, in the appendix's terms, the beginning of actually reading the work. Primary text:
